title: Nouns and Pronouns
shortDescription: Naming words and their stand-ins — countable vs uncountable, and every pronoun type that examiners love to test.
genZNote: Nouns name the world; pronouns are the world's nicknames so you don't have to keep repeating yourself.

rows: chair(s), idea(s) — can be counted, take a/an and plural -s
water, furniture, information, advice — no plural, no a/an
honesty, freedom, courage — an idea/quality, not a physical thing

sections.heading: Countable vs uncountable — the exam traps
bullets: Uncountable nouns never take 'a/an' and never take a plural -s: say 'much information', never 'an information' or 'informations'.
Common uncountable nouns that LOOK plural or countable: advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, information, news, knowledge, equipment, homework, bread.
'News' looks plural but takes a SINGULAR verb: 'The news is good' (not 'are good').
Some nouns change meaning between countable and uncountable: 'a paper' (a newspaper/an exam paper) vs 'paper' (the material).

sections.heading: Collective nouns — singular or plural verb?
bullets: A collective noun (team, family, jury, committee, government) usually takes a SINGULAR verb when acting as one unit: 'The team is playing well.'
It can take a PLURAL verb when members are acting/thought of as individuals: 'The team are arguing among themselves.'
Indian competitive exams default to the singular-unit reading unless the sentence clearly signals individual disagreement.

rows: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
Stands in for a specific person/thing
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
Shows ownership, used alone (not before a noun)
Subject and object are the same person
Introduces a relative clause, links back to a noun

sections.heading: who / whom / which / that — how to choose
bullets: 'Who' refers to people and does the action (subject): 'the man who called'.
'Whom' refers to people and receives the action (object): 'the man whom I met' — quick test: if you can replace it with 'him', use 'whom'; if with 'he', use 'who'.
'Which' refers to things/animals, and introduces non-essential info often set off by commas: 'the book, which I bought yesterday, is great.'
'That' refers to people or things, and introduces essential info with NO comma: 'the book that I bought is great.'
A common exam error: using 'which' for a person, or 'that' after a comma.

sections.heading: Pronoun-antecedent agreement
bullets: A pronoun must agree in number and gender with the noun it replaces (its 'antecedent'): 'Each student must submit HIS OR HER assignment' (not 'their', in strict formal usage, though 'their' as a gender-neutral singular is now widely accepted).
Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone', 'somebody', 'each' are grammatically singular, so the pronoun that refers back to them is traditionally singular too: 'Everyone should bring his/her own lunch.'
Watch for a pronoun with an unclear antecedent — 'Ravi told Sunil that he had passed' is ambiguous about who 'he' is; exams flag this as a sentence-improvement error.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Nouns name people/places/things/ideas; pronouns replace nouns — both come in several types that exams test through countability, collective-noun verb agreement, and who/whom/which/that choices.
keyFacts: Uncountable nouns (advice, furniture, information, news) never take a/an or a plural -s.
Collective nouns take a singular verb as one unit, plural when members act individually.
who = subject/people, whom = object/people, which = things (non-essential), that = people or things (essential, no comma).
commonConfusion: 'Advice' vs 'advise' — advice is the uncountable NOUN, advise is the VERB.
'News' looks plural but is grammatically singular.

highYieldFacts: The who/him, whom/he memory trick resolves most who-vs-whom questions instantly.
commonTraps: Writing 'an informations' or 'furnitures' — both are uncountable and never pluralise.
Using 'which' to refer to a person instead of 'who'/'that'.
Treating 'the team are' as always wrong — it's correct when members act individually.
mustRemember: 'That' clauses are essential (no comma); 'which' clauses are extra information (comma before).

confusedTerms.distinction: 'Who' is a subject pronoun (does the action); 'whom' is an object pronoun (receives the action). Substitute he/him to test.
'Which' adds non-essential info and is set off by commas; 'that' adds essential info with no comma and can refer to people or things.

possibleQuestions: Identify the error: 'She gave me many advices about the interview.'
Choose the correct word: 'The jury ___ divided in its opinion.' (is/are)
